guides.title: Football Formations and Tactical Systems
guides.summary: How football formations like 4-4-2, 4-3-3 and 3-5-2 actually work, where they came from, and how tactical systems such as pressing, counter-attacking and possession play decide matches.

sections.heading: What a Formation Is and What It Is Not
sections.body:
A football formation is the arrangement of the ten outfield players across the pitch, described from the defensive line forward. When commentators say a team plays 4-4-2, they mean four defenders, four midfielders and two forwards, with the goalkeeper taken for granted. The numbers always add up to ten. That simple description, however, hides almost everything interesting about how a team actually plays, and the first lesson of tactical literacy is learning what a formation does and does not tell you.

A formation is best understood as a set of starting reference points rather than fixed stations. Players do not stand in their slots for ninety minutes; they move constantly, and a snapshot taken at any given moment rarely matches the diagram in the match program. What the formation provides is a default structure: who is responsible for which zone, who covers for whom when a teammate leaves position, and what passing angles exist when the team has the ball. A pitch is roughly 105 metres long and 68 metres wide, which is far too much ground for ten players to cover evenly. A formation is really a decision about where to concentrate players and where to accept space, and every choice trades coverage in one area for exposure in another.

The second thing a formation cannot tell you is how a team behaves in different phases of play. Modern analysts divide a match into four phases: established possession, established defense, the transition from attack to defense, and the transition from defense to attack. A team listed as 4-3-3 might defend in a compact 4-5-1, with its wingers dropping alongside the midfield, and attack in something closer to a 2-3-5, with full-backs pushed high and a midfielder dropping between the centre-backs. The listed formation is often just the shape the team takes at kick-off and at goal kicks, which is why average-position maps generated from tracking data frequently look nothing like the nominal system.

It is also worth separating three words that are often used interchangeably: formation, system and style. The formation is the geometric arrangement. The system is the set of behaviors layered onto it, such as whether the full-backs overlap or tuck inside, whether the team presses high or retreats, and which midfielder drops to receive the ball. The style is the broader identity, such as possession-oriented, counter-attacking or direct. Two teams can share a formation and play utterly different football. A 4-4-2 in the hands of Arrigo Sacchi's AC Milan meant a suffocating high press and an aggressive offside trap; the same numbers under a relegation-threatened side might mean two deep banks of four and long balls to a target man.

Finally, formations are relative, not absolute. Their strengths and weaknesses only exist in relation to the opponent's shape. A midfield three will usually outnumber a midfield two in the centre; a back four can be stretched by a front three's width. Coaches think in terms of these matchups, asking where their spare player is and where the opponent's is. Everything else in this guide builds on that idea: a formation is a tool for creating favorable numbers and angles somewhere on the pitch while managing the risk of being outnumbered somewhere else.

sections.heading: Reading the Numbers: The Grammar of 4-4-2, 4-3-3 and 4-2-3-1
sections.body:
Formation notation reads from the back line forward and omits the goalkeeper. The first digit counts the defenders, the last counts the forwards, and everything in between describes the midfield bands. A 4-4-2 has two lines of four and a strike pair. A 4-3-3 has a back four, a midfield triangle and three forwards. When a formation contains distinct sub-lines, modern notation splits them out: 4-2-3-1 means a back four, two holding midfielders, a band of three attacking midfielders and a lone striker. The older habit of compressing everything into three numbers survives in casual speech, which is why the same team can be described as 4-5-1 by one observer and 4-2-3-1 by another without either being wrong.

Within each band, positions have conventional names. A back four consists of two centre-backs flanked by a right-back and a left-back, collectively the full-backs. In a midfield four, the wide players are usually called wide midfielders or wingers depending on how high they play, and the central pair splits duties between destruction and creation. In a midfield three, the deepest player is the holding midfielder, defensive midfielder or pivot; the two ahead are often called the number eights. The band of three in a 4-2-3-1 contains two wide attackers and a central attacking midfielder, the classic number ten.

Those shirt-number nicknames deserve a short explanation because they carry real tactical meaning. In the traditional English numbering that grew out of the 2-3-5 era, the number nine was the centre-forward, and to this day a target striker is called a nine, while a striker who drops into midfield to link play is a false nine. The number ten was the inside-left, which evolved into the creative playmaker's shirt, worn by Pelé, Diego Maradona, Zinedine Zidane and Lionel Messi. The number six in most European countries denotes the holding midfielder, though in England the six was historically a centre-back and in Brazil the volante fills the role. When a coach says they need a proper six, they are talking about a role, not a squad number.

Notation has real limits, and learning them is part of reading the game. First, symmetry is assumed but rarely real: many teams play with one full-back attacking and the other tucking in, producing a lopsided shape that no tidy string of digits captures. Second, the numbers say nothing about height or distance. Two teams can both play 4-4-2 with one defending on the halfway line and the other on the edge of its own penalty area, and the practical difference between those two teams is enormous. Third, the numbers describe only one phase. Analysts therefore often quote two shapes, saying a team attacks in 3-2-5 and defends in 4-4-2, which has become common practice in coverage of positional-play sides.

A useful exercise for a new student of the game is to watch ten minutes of a match and simply track one band, counting how often the nominal midfield four is actually a recognizable line of four. The answer is usually less than half the time, and the gaps between the diagram and the reality are exactly where tactics live. The notation is a shared vocabulary, not a description of truth, and every serious tactical conversation starts by agreeing on which phase of play is being described.

sections.heading: The Pyramid: 2-3-5 and the Victorian Origins of Team Shape
sections.body:
The earliest organized football of the 1860s and 1870s barely had formations at all. The dominant style was the dribbling game: a player ran with the ball until dispossessed while teammates massed around him, and lineups amounted to something like 1-1-8 or 1-2-7, a wall of forwards behind a couple of defenders. Passing was considered almost unsporting in parts of the English public-school game. The change came largely from Scotland, where clubs such as Queen's Park of Glasgow developed a deliberate short-passing style, and the international matches between Scotland and England from 1872 onward showcased the superiority of combination play over solo dribbling.

As passing spread, teams pulled players back to balance the side, and by the 1880s the standard shape across Britain had settled into 2-3-5, known ever after as the pyramid. Two full-backs defended, three half-backs occupied the middle, and five forwards attacked: two wingers, two inside-forwards and a centre-forward. Preston North End, the Invincibles who won the first Football League title in 1888-89 without losing a match, played the pyramid, and it remained the near-universal formation of world football for around forty years. The formation gave the game the positional names still in use, and the numbering of shirts one to eleven, introduced widely in the 1920s and 1930s, followed the pyramid's layout, which is why the conventions described in the previous section exist at all.

The key figure in the pyramid was the centre-half, a position whose meaning has drifted so far that the original sense surprises modern fans. The centre-half of the 2-3-5 was not a defender but the fulcrum of the whole team: the middle of the three half-backs, expected to break up attacks, carry the ball forward, distribute to the wings and arrive in the box to score. He was often the best player on the team and the tactical brain of the side. The gradual demotion of the centre-half into a pure defender is the story of the next section, and the modern term centre-back preserves the fossil of that older role.

The pyramid depended on the offside law as it stood before 1925, which required three opposing players, in practice the goalkeeper and both full-backs, between the attacker and the goal line at the moment the ball was played. Clever full-back pairs learned to spring the trap by stepping up in staggered fashion, and Newcastle United's Bill McCracken became notorious for compressing play into a strip of midfield and strangling matches. Attendances and goals suffered, and the pressure this trap created on the game's spectacle led directly to the law change that killed the pyramid.

Before leaving the era, it is worth noting that the pyramid traveled. British sailors, engineers and teachers exported the game, and South America absorbed the 2-3-5 and refashioned it. Uruguay won Olympic gold in 1924 and 1928 and the first World Cup in 1930 playing a pyramid animated by short passing and individual skill, and Argentine and Uruguayan writers of the period celebrated a creole style, la nuestra, that contrasted with British muscularity. The pyramid was thus the first global tactical language, and every later system is a descendant of it, produced by pulling one or another of its five forwards progressively deeper.

sections.heading: The WM: Herbert Chapman and the 1925 Offside Revolution
sections.body:
In 1925 the game's lawmakers changed the offside rule: an attacker now needed only two defenders between himself and the goal line, not three. The intention was to produce more goals, and it worked immediately and dramatically; goals in the English Football League jumped from about 4,700 in the last season under the old law to over 6,300 in the first season under the new one. Defenses built around the old trap were suddenly naked, because a single full-back stepping up no longer played anyone offside, and long balls over the top became devastating. The formation that answered this crisis reshaped football for thirty years.

The answer is associated above all with Herbert Chapman, the Arsenal manager, and his veteran inside-forward Charlie Buchan, who pressed for the change after a heavy defeat at Newcastle in 1925. Chapman withdrew the centre-half from midfield and dropped him between the two full-backs as a third defender, a stopper whose job was simply to mark the opposing centre-forward. To restore numbers in midfield, one inside-forward dropped deeper, and the resulting shape was 3-2-2-3: three defenders, two wing-halves, two withdrawn inside-forwards and a front three of two wingers and a centre-forward. Sketched on paper, the defensive half formed a W and the attacking half an M, giving the system its enduring name.

Chapman's Arsenal demonstrated what the WM could do when staffed intelligently. The full-backs shifted outward to mark the wingers, the stopper handled the centre-forward, and the withdrawn inside-forward became the side's creator. Alex James, a small Scot with superb vision, played that role for Arsenal as a deep-lying playmaker, collecting the ball from defense and releasing fast wingers such as Cliff Bastin into the space behind squads still organized for the old game. Arsenal won the FA Cup in 1930 and five league titles across the 1930s, and Chapman, who died suddenly in 1934 midway through the run, is remembered as the first modern manager: he argued for floodlights, numbered shirts and European competition decades before they arrived.

The WM was not the only response to the new law. In Italy, Vittorio Pozzo built the Metodo, a 2-3-2-3 that kept the old two-man defense but withdrew both inside-forwards, producing a sturdier midfield and a devastating counter-attacking structure. Pozzo's Italy won the World Cups of 1934 and 1938, the only side to retain the trophy until Brazil in 1962, and the Metodo's emphasis on soaking pressure and striking quickly left a lasting mark on Italian football culture. In central Europe, the Austrian Wunderteam and the Hungarians kept an attacking centre-half far longer, and their fluid interpretation of the old pyramid would eventually produce the side that humiliated WM England.

That humiliation is the hinge of tactical history. In November 1953 Hungary came to Wembley and beat England 6-3, then won the return in Budapest 7-1. Gusztáv Sebes's side listed a 2-3-3-2 variant in which the nominal centre-forward, Nándor Hidegkuti, dropped deep into midfield. England's stopper centre-back, trained by decades of WM to mark the number nine, followed him and left a hole, or stayed and left him free; either way the system collapsed. The lesson, that a rigid man-marking scheme dies against intelligent movement, ended the WM's reign and opened the door to the back four and the deep-lying forward, the raw material of everything that followed.

sections.heading: Catenaccio and the Libero: The Art of the Door-Bolt
sections.body:
Catenaccio, Italian for door-bolt, is the most notorious defensive system in football history, and like many notorious things it is widely misdescribed. Its mechanical origins lie not in Italy but in Switzerland, where the Austrian coach Karl Rappan, working with Servette and the Swiss national team in the 1930s, devised the verrou, or bolt. Rappan's problem was that his part-time players could not match professional opponents athletically, so he substituted organization for athleticism: he withdrew a player behind the main defensive line as a permanent spare man, covering whoever was beaten. Switzerland's defeat of much-fancied Germany at the 1938 World Cup advertised the idea to the world.

In Italy the spare man became the libero, the free man, also called the sweeper because he swept up behind his man-marking teammates. Nereo Rocco proved the system's worth with unfashionable Triestina, then won the European Cup with AC Milan in 1963. But catenaccio's defining team was Helenio Herrera's Internazionale, the Grande Inter of the mid-1960s. Herrera, an Argentine-born showman and one of the first managers to become a bigger celebrity than his players, set up with man-markers across the defense, Armando Picchi sweeping behind them, and Giacinto Facchetti, a tall left-back with a sprinter's stride, surging forward as one of the game's first genuinely attacking full-backs. Inter won back-to-back European Cups in 1964 and 1965 and two league titles, defending narrow leads with a discipline that opponents found suffocating.

The caricature of catenaccio is ten men behind the ball and cynical time-wasting, and the late-period Inter sometimes earned it. But the system was a coherent attacking proposition as well: by committing five or six players to fixed defensive duties it freed the remainder for rapid counter-attacks into the space that frustrated opponents left behind. The libero, facing the play with no direct opponent, was ideally placed to start those counters with long diagonal passes. The bolt was a spring as much as a lock, and the Italian tradition of the lightning transition, visible decades later in sides such as Mourinho's treble-winning Inter of 2010, descends directly from it.

The libero role itself outgrew the system that created it. Franz Beckenbauer, at Bayern Munich and with the West Germany team that won the 1972 European Championship and the 1974 World Cup, reinvented the sweeper as an attacking position, striding out of defense into midfield to create overloads, secure in the knowledge that the man-markers behind him held their opponents. The elegant ball-playing libero remained a fixture of German and Italian football into the 1990s, with Lothar Matthäus and Franco Baresi offering contrasting late examples, and the modern ball-playing centre-back who steps into midfield is the role's direct heir.

Catenaccio died at home. Arrigo Sacchi, taking over AC Milan in 1987, declared war on the entire Italian defensive inheritance, abolishing the libero and man-marking in favor of a zonal back four, a high line and collective pressing. His Milan won the European Cup in 1989 and 1990 and persuaded Italy that the future lay elsewhere. Yet the deeper lessons of the bolt survive everywhere: the value of a spare man at the back, the power of the counter-attack, and the truth that a well-organized inferior team can beat a superior one. Every coach who parks the bus and breaks at speed is quoting Rappan and Herrera, whether they know it or not.

sections.heading: Total Football: Ajax, Cruyff and the Idea of Universal Players
sections.body:
Total Football is the name attached to the style developed at Ajax of Amsterdam under Rinus Michels between 1965 and 1971 and carried to its peak by the Netherlands national team at the 1974 World Cup. Its core idea is positional interchange: any outfield player may take over the role of any other, provided the team's overall structure is preserved. When the left-back surges seventy metres into attack, a midfielder drops into his place; when the centre-forward wanders to the wing, someone fills the central space. Positions belong to the team's shape, not to individuals, and the player is expected to read the whole game rather than a single role.

The system rested on two mechanical foundations that are easy to miss beneath the romance. The first was the manipulation of space. Michels's teams made the pitch enormous in possession, spreading wide and deep so that every pass had options, and tiny out of possession, squeezing forty metres of effective playing space into which opponents were pressed the moment the ball was lost. The second was the offside trap and a startlingly high defensive line, which compressed play toward the opponent's goal and let Ajax defend in the other team's half. Pressing, a defensive act, was thus the engine of an attacking style, a paradox that reappears in every pressing system since.

Johan Cruyff was the system's on-field intelligence, nominally a centre-forward but in practice appearing everywhere, directing teammates with constant gesture and instruction. Around him Ajax fielded technically complete players such as Johan Neeskens, Ruud Krol and Piet Keizer, raised by the club's youth system to be comfortable in any zone. Ajax won three consecutive European Cups in 1971, 1972 and 1973, and the 1974 Dutch national side, largely built on Ajax and Feyenoord players, produced some of the most admired football ever played on the way to the final, including a first-minute penalty in that final against West Germany before a Dutch teammate other than the Germans had touched the ball. The Netherlands lost 2-1, and the defeat fixed the team in memory as the greatest side never to win the World Cup.

Total Football's demands explain its rarity. It requires eleven players of high technical skill, tactical understanding and exceptional fitness, plus a culture that tolerates defenders attacking and forwards defending. It also requires years of shared education; the interchanges only work when every player reads the same pictures. This is why the style has flourished mainly where a single club controls player development over a long period, and why its purest revivals have come through the Ajax school and its exports rather than through imitation from a distance.

The lineage, however, is the most influential in football. Cruyff took the ideas to Barcelona as a player in 1973 and returned as coach in 1988, building the Dream Team that won the club's first European Cup in 1992 and founding the pedagogical program at La Masia that later produced Xavi, Andrés Iniesta and Lionel Messi. Cruyff's pupil Pep Guardiola systematized the inheritance into modern positional play. The Dutch 4-3-3, the ball-playing goalkeeper, the pressing trigger, the midfielder dropping between centre-backs: all of it descends from the Amsterdam of 1970. Total Football is less a formation than a philosophy, and it remains the game's most fertile one.

sections.heading: The 4-4-2: Two Banks of Four and the Power of Compactness
sections.body:
The 4-4-2 is the plainest of the classic formations and for decades was the default across Britain and much of Europe. Its geometry is two flat lines of four, defense and midfield, with a pair of strikers ahead. Every player has a mirror partner and a clear zone, the spacing is symmetrical, and the shape provides natural width on both flanks and two players permanently near the opponent's goal. For coaches, its great virtue is teachability: the roles are simple to explain, the covering patterns are intuitive, and a newly assembled team can reach organizational competence in a 4-4-2 faster than in almost any other shape.

The formation's defensive logic is compactness. When the two banks of four stay close together, perhaps twenty-five to thirty metres from the deepest defender to the forwards, and shift side to side as a unit, they close the central corridors through which dangerous passes travel and force play into wide areas, where the touchline acts as an extra defender. The strikers curve their runs to steer the opponent's build-up one way, and the ball-side midfielder steps out while his three partners slide across. Taught well, this produces a defensive machine requiring no exceptional athletes, which is why the 4-4-2 mid-block remains a refuge of underdogs everywhere. Diego Simeone's Atlético Madrid, champions of Spain in 2014 and 2021 and twice Champions League finalists, are the modern reference: a ferociously drilled 4-4-2 that concedes the flanks, blocks the middle and breaks with brutal directness.

The formation's attacking identity historically centered on the strike partnership, one of football's most productive relationships. Classic pairings combined complementary types: a target man to win long balls and hold possession beside a quick poacher running beyond him, or a deep-dropping second striker linking midfield to a penalty-box finisher. Wide midfielders supplied crosses, and the far-side winger attacked the back post. Leicester City's improbable Premier League title in 2015-16 was built on exactly this ancient pattern: a compact 4-4-2, Jamie Vardy sprinting behind defenses, and rapid transitions through N'Golo Kanté's ball-winning.

The most celebrated 4-4-2 of all was anything but conservative. Arrigo Sacchi's AC Milan of 1987 to 1991, European champions in 1989 and 1990, used the shape as a pressing instrument. Sacchi abolished the Italian libero, defended zonally with a back four holding a line sometimes near halfway, and demanded that the whole team squeeze within twenty-five metres, hunting the ball collectively with an aggressive offside trap behind them. His famous training reference points, ball, opponent, teammate and space, taught players to position themselves by multiple cues rather than simply following a man. Sacchi proved a formation's numbers say nothing about its ambition, and his ideas shaped a generation of coaches including many with no other Italian inheritance.

The 4-4-2's weaknesses drove its decline as elite fashion. A central midfield pair is outnumbered by the three of a 4-3-3 or 4-2-3-1, and the space between the two banks, if they separate, is exactly where a number ten lives. The answer of the 1990s was the diamond midfield, tilting the four into a holding player, two shuttlers and a playmaker at the tip, buying central numbers at the cost of width. At the highest level the flat 4-4-2 is now mostly a defensive shape that teams adopt out of possession, but as such it may still be the most-used arrangement in world football on any given weekend.

sections.heading: The 4-3-3 and the Midfield Triangle
sections.body:
The 4-3-3 arranges a back four, a midfield triangle and a front three of a centre-forward flanked by two wingers. Its modern prestige comes from the Dutch school and from Barcelona, but its essential appeal is geometric: the midfield triangle creates passing angles that flat lines cannot, and the front three stretches the opponent's back four across the full width of the pitch. It is the formation most associated with possession football, though it serves pressing and counter-attacking sides just as well.

The triangle usually points backward: a single holding midfielder, the pivot or number six, sits behind two number eights. The pivot is the team's structural key. He receives from the centre-backs under pressure, switches play, screens the space in front of the defense and breaks up counter-attacks, and the great pivots, from Sergio Busquets to Rodri, are valued less for tackles than for the ability to receive on the half-turn in traffic and choose the right forward pass. The eights carry the ball through midfield, arrive in the penalty area and press the opponent's build-up. The triangle can also be inverted, with two holders behind one attacking midfielder, which trades attacking presence for security and shades the shape toward 4-2-3-1.

The front three defines the formation's width. Classic wingers hug the touchlines, pinning the opposing full-backs and isolating them for one-against-one dribbles, which keeps the central channels open for the eights. The inverted winger, a left-footer on the right or right-footer on the left, cuts inside to shoot or combine, and his full-back overlaps outside to provide the width instead. The centre-forward may be a conventional nine attacking crosses and running the channels, or a false nine who drops into midfield to create a numerical surplus there. The most famous false nine experiment came in May 2009, when Pep Guardiola moved Lionel Messi from the right wing into the withdrawn central role away to Real Madrid; Barcelona won 6-2, and the role anchored the side that many regard as the best club team ever assembled.

Guardiola's Barcelona of 2008 to 2012, built on the pivot Busquets, the eights Xavi and Iniesta and Messi's false nine, gave the 4-3-3 its modern aura, winning two Champions Leagues and three league titles with a suffocating combination of possession and instant counter-pressing. A different 4-3-3 conquered Europe under Jürgen Klopp at Liverpool: a hard-running triangle behind a narrow, aggressive front three of Mohamed Salah, Roberto Firmino and Sadio Mané, with width supplied almost entirely by the full-backs Trent Alexander-Arnold and Andy Robertson. Liverpool won the Champions League in 2019 and the league title in 2020, demonstrating the same numbers serving a transition-based identity rather than a possession one.

The formation's vulnerabilities are the mirror of its strengths. The single pivot can be swamped by two opponents between the lines, which is why teams facing a 4-3-3 often field a number ten directly on the six, and the high, wide wingers leave the full-backs to defend large spaces behind them in transition. Sides that beat great 4-3-3 teams have usually done it by attacking the channels either side of the pivot quickly, before the eights recover. The standard modern answers are a second holding player in big away matches, or the in-possession rearrangement into a 3-2-5, in which a full-back steps into midfield beside the pivot, a structure covered later in this guide.

sections.heading: The 4-2-3-1 and the Age of the Number Ten
sections.body:
The 4-2-3-1 was the signature formation of the 2000s and early 2010s, at one point so prevalent that entire international tournaments seemed to be contested between mirror images of it. Its structure layers a back four, a double pivot of two holding midfielders, a band of three attacking midfielders and a lone striker. The system's appeal is balance: it offers the central security of two holders, the width of two wide attackers, a dedicated creator between the lines and a clear reference point up front, and it converts neatly into two banks of four when possession is lost, with the wide attackers dropping alongside the pivots and the number ten joining the striker.

The double pivot is the formation's foundation and comes in recognizable flavors. A destroyer-distributor pairing couples a ball-winner with a deep passer, the model of Claude Makélélé beside a creator at Chelsea, and Makélélé's influence there was so pronounced that the deepest midfield position is still sometimes called the Makélélé role in England. Other pairings use two all-rounders who take turns stepping forward. Whatever the mix, one pivot must always remain behind the ball, and the discipline of that rotation is the difference between a solid 4-2-3-1 and a leaky one.

The number ten is the formation's glamour role and its reason for existing. Operating in the pocket between the opponent's midfield and defense, the ten receives between the lines, turns, and plays the final pass. The 4-2-3-1 era was the golden age of such players, with Mesut Özil, Wesley Sneijder, Kaká and Juan Román Riquelme organizing attacks from the pocket while two runners stretched play either side. Sneijder's Internazionale under José Mourinho won the treble in 2010 with a counter-attacking 4-2-3-1, and Spain won the 2010 World Cup and Germany the 2014 edition from starting shapes generally described the same way, though Spain's version blurred into a 4-3-3 through Xavi's positioning.

Out of possession, the 4-2-3-1 gave coaches a ready-made 4-4-1-1 medium block, and its pressing scheme wrote itself: the striker screens the pivot, the ten presses the centre-backs, and the wide players jump onto the full-backs. Mourinho's sides at Chelsea and Real Madrid showed its counter-attacking ceiling, with his 2011-12 Madrid winning La Liga with 100 points and 121 goals, most of them scored in devastating transitions through Özil, Cristiano Ronaldo and Ángel Di María. The formation rewarded fast wide players who could run sixty metres into vacated space, and for a decade it was the default vehicle for exactly that profile.

The system declined at the very top for one main reason: the space the number ten needs began to disappear. Pressing improved, midfields compressed, and holding midfielders learned to defend the pocket zonally rather than following runners out of it. A ten who does not defend leaves his double pivot outnumbered against a midfield three, and elite coaches increasingly preferred the 4-3-3's extra central body or hybrid shapes that generate a ten positionally rather than by nomination. Yet the 4-2-3-1 remains among the most common formations in professional football, particularly for teams that want defensive structure without abandoning a creator, and its vocabulary, the double pivot, the ten, the inverted wide man cutting in from the flank, is now simply part of how the game is described.

sections.heading: Back Threes and Wing-Backs: 3-5-2, 3-4-3 and the Back Five
sections.body:
Systems with three centre-backs form football's second great family of shapes. Their logic differs fundamentally from the back four: the wide defensive duties belong not to full-backs within the line but to wing-backs stationed higher, each responsible for an entire flank in both directions, while the three central defenders share the width of the penalty area. Depending on where the wing-backs stand at a given moment, the same team reads as 3-5-2 in attack and 5-3-2 in defense, and this elasticity is the family's defining feature rather than a contradiction.

The modern back three's breakthrough came at the 1986 World Cup, where Carlos Bilardo's Argentina won the tournament in a 3-5-2 built to give Diego Maradona a platform. Bilardo reasoned that since opponents attacked with two strikers, three defenders sufficed to mark them with a spare man, releasing an extra body into midfield. Franz Beckenbauer's West Germany reached the same final with a sweeper system of similar arithmetic and won the next World Cup in 1990 with it, and through the 1990s the 3-5-2 flourished wherever strike pairs remained standard, notably in Serie A and the Bundesliga. Its later fading followed the strikers: when 4-2-3-1 made the lone forward universal, three markers against one striker became a waste, and the back three nearly vanished from elite football in the 2000s.

Its revival is one of recent history's clearest tactical stories. Antonio Conte's Juventus, unbeaten champions of Italy in 2011-12 and winners of three straight titles, rebuilt the 3-5-2 around a midfield of Andrea Pirlo, Arturo Vidal and Claudio Marchisio, with Giorgio Chiellini, Leonardo Bonucci and Andrea Barzagli forming the league's best defense and Bonucci's long diagonal passing turning the spare defender into a playmaker. Conte then joined Chelsea, began the 2016-17 season in a back four, was beaten 3-0 by Arsenal in September, switched to 3-4-3, won thirteen consecutive league matches and the title, and set off a wave of back-three adoption across the Premier League. The 3-4-3 variant flattens the midfield to two and plays two attackers off a central striker, trading a central body for more permanent forward presence.

The system's advantages cluster around build-up and the flanks. Against a single pressing striker, three defenders always include a free man to carry the ball forward. The wing-backs provide width without requiring wingers, which suits squads rich in central players, and against teams whose width comes from full-backs, wing-backs engage them directly and neutralize the supply. Defensively the shape collapses into a back five that is extremely difficult to play through or cross against, which is why back fives dominate among underdogs in knockout football and among national teams with limited preparation time.

The costs are equally specific. Wing-back is among the most demanding roles in the sport, requiring a player to deliver crosses like a winger and recover like a full-back for ninety minutes, and a team without two genuine specialists compromises somewhere. Against opponents who pin the wing-backs deep with high wingers, the shape degenerates into a passive 5-3-2 with isolated forwards, the caricature its critics attack. And the three centre-backs must be comfortable defending wide areas when a wing-back is beaten, a skill classic central defenders often lack. The back three is thus neither defensive nor attacking in itself; it is a different way of distributing the same ten players, whose character depends entirely on the heights at which its wing-backs live.

sections.heading: Out of Possession: Pressing, Blocks and the Counter-Press
sections.body:
A team's defensive system is a separate decision from its formation, and modern tactical language describes it chiefly by the height of the defensive block. A high press engages the opponent's build-up near their penalty area; a mid-block concedes the first third and defends around halfway; a low block retreats to the edge of its own area and defends the spaces closest to goal. Each height trades risk for opportunity differently. Pressing high can win the ball thirty metres from goal, the most valuable turnovers in football, but leaves enormous space behind the defensive line; a low block surrenders territory and invites pressure but offers opponents almost no room for the final pass.

Organized pressing is built on triggers and traps rather than constant chasing, which no team can sustain. Common triggers include a pass backward, a poor first touch, a ball played to the touchline where the presser's cover shadow and the sideline cage the receiver, and a pass to a player known to be weak under pressure. Pressing players approach on curved runs that block the pass back inside, using the cover shadow, the space blocked behind the presser's body, to remove options while attacking the ball. A pressing trap deliberately leaves one pass open, then converges on the receiver the moment the ball travels. Analysts measure pressing intensity with PPDA, opponent passes allowed per defensive action, where low numbers indicate aggression.

Gegenpressing, or counter-pressing, is the specialized art of pressing in the seconds immediately after losing the ball, rather than retreating into shape. Its rationale, articulated most famously by Jürgen Klopp, is that the moment of transition is the opponent's most vulnerable: the winning team's players have spread to attack, their structure momentarily broken, and the player who has just won the ball is focused on it and poorly oriented. Klopp called counter-pressing the best playmaker in the world, because a ball won there is already among disorganized opponents near their goal. His Borussia Dortmund sides won consecutive Bundesliga titles in 2011 and 2012 on the method, and his Liverpool refined it into a Champions League and Premier League winner. Guardiola's teams practice a version bounded by rules, pressing intensely for the first few seconds after loss and falling back into shape if the ball is not recovered.

At the other pole, the deep block remains one of football's most effective and least loved systems. Mourinho's Internazionale eliminated Guardiola's Barcelona in the 2010 Champions League semi-final defending for long stretches with ten men behind the ball, completing famously few passes at the Camp Nou while conceding once across the tie's decisive phases, and Atlético Madrid under Simeone turned the compact 4-4-2 mid-to-low block into a decade-long identity. Good blocks are not passive: they maintain horizontal compactness by shifting as a unit, keep the distance between lines short enough that no opponent can turn between them, and choreograph which passes they allow, usually sideways and backward ones.

Marking schemes cut across all block heights. Pure zonal defending assigns spaces, pure man-marking assigns opponents, and almost every real system mixes them, defending zonally until an opponent enters the zone and then engaging man to man. The extreme experiment is Marcelo Bielsa's man-to-man press across the entire pitch, in which every player follows an assigned opponent everywhere, a scheme of thrilling intensity and famous fragility, since a single lost duel creates a free man with no cover behind. Where a team sets its block, and how it marks within it, says more about its real identity than the formation ever does.

sections.heading: In Possession: Positional Play, Tiki-Taka and Direct Football
sections.body:
Attacking systems divide broadly into those that progress the ball through controlled possession and those that progress it quickly at the cost of control. The most influential possession doctrine is positional play, juego de posición, the framework refined by Pep Guardiola from Cruyff's inheritance. The pitch is divided into a grid of zones, most famously five vertical corridors: two wings, two half-spaces, the valuable channels between the wide and central lanes, and the centre. Rules govern occupation, in the classic formulation no more than two players in the same horizontal line and no more than three in the same vertical corridor, guaranteeing staggered positions, constant triangles and a free man somewhere. The aim is not possession for its own sake but the manipulation of the opponent: overload one side to draw defenders, then switch to the isolated winger, or draw the press onto short passes to open the pocket behind it for the third man.

Tiki-taka, the name attached to Spain's international sides of 2008 to 2012, was this school's most decorated expression. Built on Barcelona's midfield of Xavi Hernández, Andrés Iniesta and Sergio Busquets, Spain won the European Championships of 2008 and 2012 and the 2010 World Cup, the first nation ever to win three consecutive major tournaments, completing pass totals opponents could not approach and defending largely by never giving the ball away. Critics called late-period tiki-taka sterile, and Guardiola himself has bristled at the word, insisting that passing without penetration betrays the idea. The distinction matters: positional play treats possession as a means of disorganizing the opponent, and its metric is progress toward goal, not pass count.

The doctrine's structural signature today is the build-up shape. Teams construct attacks from the goalkeeper, whose feet are now a selection criterion, through a first line designed to beat the opponent's press with a spare man: two centre-backs splitting wide with the pivot between them, or a 3-2 base formed when a full-back steps inside, the inverted full-back role Guardiola created for Philipp Lahm at Bayern Munich in 2013 and later gave to João Cancelo and John Stones at Manchester City. Ahead of that base, five players typically occupy the five corridors, producing the 3-2-5 attacking shape that has become the sport's contemporary default at the elite level. Guardiola's Manchester City won the Premier League with 100 points in 2018 and completed the treble in 2023 on successive versions of this structure.

Direct football is the honest opposite: move the ball forward early, before the opponent's defense is set. Its crude form is the long ball to a target man with runners gambling on flicks and second balls, a style associated in England with coaches such as Tony Pulis and long effective at limiting the influence of superior opponents. Its sophisticated form is the vertical transition game: win possession, and within two or three passes put a runner into the space behind the defense. Counter-attacking sides accept long defensive phases as the price of attacking against a broken structure, the most valuable situation in football, and history's list of great counter-attacking teams, from Herrera's Inter to Mourinho's Madrid to Leicester's champions, is as distinguished as the possession canon.

No elite team is purely one or the other. Possession sides rest-defend against counters even while attacking, positioning two or three players behind the ball specifically to counter-press a loss, and counter-attacking sides must hold the ball well enough to breathe. The stylistic argument that runs through football history, control against chaos, is really an argument about which risks a coach prefers, and the best teams of every era have been fluent in both languages.

sections.heading: Choosing a System: Matchups, Player Fit and In-Game Management
sections.body:
There is no best formation, and the surest sign of tactical illiteracy is the belief that one exists. A system is a compromise among the players available, the opponent's shape, the competition context and the coach's convictions, and the craft lies in weighing those factors honestly. The first and heaviest is player fit. A 3-5-2 without genuine wing-backs, a 4-3-3 without a pivot who can receive under pressure, a counter-attacking plan without pace up front: each is a diagram waiting to fail. Most good coaches begin from their best players and build a structure that maximizes them, rather than importing a fashionable shape and forcing the squad into it.

The second factor is the matchup, analyzed as a search for spare men and overloads. Set any two formations against each other and the arithmetic falls out zone by zone: a 4-3-3's midfield triangle outnumbers a 4-4-2's central pair three against two; a 3-5-2's spare centre-back beats a lone striker's press; two strikers against a back three leave a free defender, which is precisely why the back three faded when lone-striker systems became universal. Coaches game-plan by locating the opponent's free man and deciding either to accept him in a harmless zone, to sacrifice a player from another zone to mark him, or to change shape so the numbers fall differently. The pre-match formation choice is largely this calculation, made with imperfect information about what the opponent will actually do.

Training is where a formation becomes a system. Teams rehearse patterns of play, repeatable passing sequences out of the build-up, rotations in which three players interchange along a flank, set pressing schemes against the opponent's expected structure, until the decisions become what coaches call automatisms, executed without deliberation. The weekly cycle in a professional club typically moves from recovery through tactical themes to an opponent-specific rehearsal, and the quality of that unseen work, more than the choice of numbers, separates organized teams from confused ones. A useful rule of thumb: a team can only play as complex a system as it has had time to train.

In-game management is the visible tip of the craft. Trailing teams add attackers and accept structural risk, most conventionally by moving to a back three that pushes an extra body forward, or simply by loading the box for crosses in the final minutes. Leading teams protect the middle, add fresh legs on the flanks and stretch the game's remaining minutes. Substitutions are also structural moves: a fresh winger against a tiring full-back is the classic targeted change. Conte's mid-season switch of Chelsea to 3-4-3 in 2016, which turned a stuttering side into champions within weeks, is the standard modern example of a formation change transforming a season, and half-time adjustments, a marking change, a swapped flank, a dropped line, decide far more matches than team sheets do.

For a coach at any level, from Sunday league to academy, the practical advice condenses to a few rules. Choose a shape your players can physically sustain; amateur wing-backs tire by the hour mark. Give every player one clear defensive job and one clear attacking job before adding nuance. Prefer principles, good spacing, immediate pressure on the ball, a spare man in build-up, to choreography, because principles survive contact with chaos and eight-year-olds should be learning the game, not memorizing a diagram. And watch the match, not the plan: the formation is where the conversation starts, and the opponent always gets a say in where it goes.

guides.title: Association Football Rules and Positions
guides.summary: A complete account of how association football is governed and played: the seventeen Laws of the Game, the field and equipment, offside, fouls and restarts, and the positional roles and formations that organise eleven players into a team.

sections.heading: What the Game Is and Who Writes the Rules
sections.body:
Association football is a game played between two teams of eleven players who attempt to put a ball into the opposing team's goal without using their hands or arms, with the sole exception of each team's goalkeeper inside a marked area near their own goal. It is the most widely played and watched sport in the world, and part of the reason is that its rulebook is short, stable and expressed in ordinary language. The entire code fits into seventeen numbered Laws, and those Laws have changed only incrementally since they were first written down. A person who understands the seventeen Laws can walk onto a pitch anywhere on earth and play. 

The rules were codified in London on 26 October 1863, when representatives of a dozen clubs and schools met at the Freemasons' Tavern to found the Football Association and agree a single set of Laws. Before that meeting, almost every school and town played a different game: the Cambridge Rules of the 1840s and the Sheffield Rules of 1858 were serious attempts at codification, but they disagreed with each other and with everyone else about handling, hacking the shins, and offside. The 1863 meeting settled the central question by voting to forbid carrying the ball in the hands and to forbid hacking, at which point the clubs that wanted those things left and eventually formed the separate code of rugby football. The word soccer is simply a nineteenth-century English slang abbreviation of the word association, formed the same way rugby football became rugger. 

Since 1886 the Laws have been owned not by any national federation but by the International Football Association Board, universally called the IFAB. It was created so that England, Scotland, Wales and Ireland could agree on a common code, and it retains an unusual constitution. The IFAB has eight votes: four belong to FIFA, the world governing body founded in 1904, and one each to the English, Scottish, Welsh and Northern Irish associations. Any change to the Laws requires six of those eight votes, which means FIFA cannot change the Laws alone and neither can the four British associations acting together. That deliberately awkward arithmetic is why the game has resisted the constant rule-tinkering common in other sports. 

The Laws are also written to be applied by a human being in real time with no equipment beyond a whistle, and they say so explicitly. Many of them turn on judgements of intent, carelessness and interference that no mechanical test could settle. A referee is instructed to use the Laws to make the game safe, fair and enjoyable, and is given discretion to let trivial infringements go. Understanding football's rules therefore means understanding both the written text and the conventions of interpretation that referees are trained to apply, because the two together are what actually governs a match.

sections.heading: The Field of Play and Its Markings
sections.body:
A football pitch is a rectangle of grass or approved artificial turf whose dimensions are given as ranges rather than fixed numbers, which is unusual among major sports and has real tactical consequences. The touchline, running the long way, must be between 90 and 120 metres (100 to 130 yards). The goal line, running the short way behind each goal, must be between 45 and 90 metres (50 to 100 yards). The touchline must always be longer than the goal line. For matches between national teams the ranges narrow considerably: 100 to 110 metres long by 64 to 75 metres wide, which is why international pitches feel more uniform than club pitches. A common professional size is 105 by 68 metres. All lines are part of the areas they bound, and they must be of the same width, no more than 12 centimetres. 

The pitch is divided in half by a halfway line with a centre mark at its midpoint, around which a circle of 9.15 metres (10 yards) radius is drawn. That radius, ten yards, recurs throughout the Laws as the standard distance opponents must retreat at a restart. Each goal sits centred on its goal line and consists of two upright posts 7.32 metres (8 yards) apart joined by a horizontal crossbar 2.44 metres (8 feet) above the ground. Posts and crossbar must be white, of the same width and depth as the goal line, and no more than 12 centimetres thick, and they must be anchored securely, a requirement written in blood after portable goals have fallen on and killed children. 

Two nested rectangles sit in front of each goal. The goal area, often called the six-yard box, extends 5.5 metres from the inside of each post and 5.5 metres into the field. The penalty area, the eighteen-yard box, extends 16.5 metres from the inside of each post and 16.5 metres into the field. Inside the penalty area a penalty mark is placed 11 metres (12 yards) from the midpoint between the posts, and outside the area an arc of 9.15 metres radius is drawn around that mark so that players know where they may not stand during a penalty kick. The penalty area is legally decisive: it defines where the goalkeeper may handle the ball and where a direct free kick offence becomes a penalty kick. 

At each corner stands a flagpost at least 1.5 metres high with a non-pointed top, and a quarter circle of one metre radius is drawn inside the field from it. Optional marks 9.15 metres from the corner arc may be made outside the goal line and touchline to help referees judge the retreat distance at corner kicks. A technical area for each team's coaching staff, and the width of the goal nets if used, are governed by competition rules rather than by the Laws themselves.

sections.heading: The Ball, the Players and the Equipment
sections.body:
The ball must be spherical, made of suitable material, between 68 and 70 centimetres in circumference, and between 410 and 450 grams in weight at the start of the match. Its pressure must be between 0.6 and 1.1 atmospheres at sea level, which is 600 to 1,100 grams per square centimetre, or roughly 8.5 to 15.6 pounds per square inch. Those tolerances matter more than they look. A ball inflated to the top of the range is harder, flies further and skids off wet grass; a soft ball dies on the first touch and rewards close control. The mass range is why a wet, muddy leather ball of the pre-1960s era, which absorbed water and could gain hundreds of grams over ninety minutes, was a genuinely different and more dangerous object to head than a modern coated synthetic one. 

A match is played by two teams of not more than eleven players, one of whom must be the goalkeeper. A match may not start, and must be abandoned if it has started, if either team has fewer than seven players on the field. That threshold, seven, is a practical compromise: it permits a team reduced by injuries and dismissals to continue but stops matches becoming farcical. Substitutions are governed by competition rules within limits set by the Laws. Most senior competitions now allow five substitutions, a change introduced as a temporary measure during the compressed fixture calendar of 2020 and written permanently into the Laws in 2022, with the restriction that they be made in a maximum of three stoppages plus half-time so that a team cannot break up play repeatedly. Additional permanent concussion substitutes are permitted in many competitions and do not count against that total. 

Compulsory equipment is a shirt with sleeves, shorts, socks, shinguards and footwear. Shinguards must be covered entirely by the socks, made of a suitable material, and provide reasonable protection: a bare tibia struck by a studded boot fractures readily, and this is the one piece of protective equipment the Laws insist on. The two teams must wear colours distinguishing them from each other, from the match officials and, in the goalkeepers' case, from all outfield players. Undershorts and undershirts, if worn, must match the main colour of the corresponding garment. 

Jewellery of every kind is forbidden, including rings, necklaces, earrings and hair beads, and taping over them is not sufficient. Any other equipment, such as headgear, face masks, knee braces or spectacles, is permitted only if it is not dangerous and has been inspected by the referee. Modern electronic performance and tracking systems, the vests containing GPS units that players wear beneath their shirts, are explicitly allowed provided they are not dangerous and, in official competitions, are approved to the relevant standard.

sections.heading: The Officials and Video Assistance
sections.body:
Every match is controlled by a referee who has full authority to enforce the Laws in connection with the match, and whose decisions regarding facts connected with play are final. That phrase is doing heavy work: it means a referee's judgement that a ball crossed a line, or that a challenge was careless, cannot be overturned by protest, and it is the reason football has historically absorbed obvious errors rather than replaying matches. A referee may change a decision only on realising it is incorrect or on the advice of another official, and only if play has not restarted or the match has not been ended. 

The referee is normally assisted by two assistant referees, one on each touchline, who patrol the halves nearest their own bench and signal when the ball leaves the field, which team is entitled to the restart, whether a player is in an offside position, and offences they see that the referee could not. The assistant on the far side from an incident often has the only clear view. A fourth official manages substitutions and the technical areas and indicates the minimum additional time. Larger competitions may add two additional assistant referees positioned behind each goal, and reserve assistant referees. 

Two technologies have been admitted into the Laws. Goal-line technology, permitted from 2012, determines automatically and within one second whether the whole of the ball has crossed the whole of the goal line, signalling to the referee's watch. It is a purely factual, binary determination, which is why it has been uncontroversial. The video assistant referee, or VAR, was written into the Laws in 2018 and is far more contested because it applies to judgement calls. VAR may intervene in only four categories of decision: goals and the offences leading up to them, penalty decisions and the offences leading up to them, direct red card incidents, and mistaken identity when a card is shown to the wrong player. 

The threshold for VAR intervention is a clear and obvious error, or a serious missed incident. The video official does not re-referee the match; the on-field referee remains the decision-maker and, for subjective calls, is expected to view the replay personally at a pitchside monitor before changing a decision. Factual matters such as whether an offside player was ahead of the second-last defender, or whether a foul occurred inside or outside the penalty area, are treated as objective and may be corrected without an on-field review. The persistent criticism of VAR is not that it is wrong more often than the naked eye but that drawing millimetre offside lines on a moving image imposes a precision the underlying evidence does not support, and that long delays damage the rhythm of a game whose appeal rests on continuous play. Semi-automated offside systems using limb tracking were introduced from 2022 partly to shorten those delays.

sections.heading: Duration, Kick-Off and Ball In and Out of Play
sections.body:
A match lasts two equal halves of 45 minutes, reduced only by agreement between the referee and the two teams before the start and only if competition rules permit. The half-time interval must not exceed 15 minutes. Time is kept by the referee, not by a stadium clock, and the clock does not stop. Instead the referee adds an allowance at the end of each half for time lost through substitutions, injuries and their treatment, time-wasting, disciplinary sanctions, drinks breaks, VAR reviews, and any other cause including significant delays at a restart such as goal celebrations. The fourth official indicates the minimum amount to be added, and the referee may add more but never less. A directive applied at the 2022 World Cup produced added times of eight and ten minutes and showed how much of the nominal ninety had been lost. 

A coin toss decides which team chooses which goal to attack in the first half; the other team takes the kick-off. In the second half the teams change ends and the team that won the toss takes the kick-off. At a kick-off all players except the kicker must be in their own half, opponents must be at least 9.15 metres from the ball until it is in play, and the ball must be stationary on the centre mark. Since 2016 the ball is in play as soon as it is kicked and clearly moves, and it may be kicked in any direction, which ended the century-old convention of a mandatory forward touch to a second player. A goal may be scored directly from a kick-off, and if it goes directly into the kicker's own goal a corner is awarded. 

The ball is out of play when it has wholly crossed the goal line or touchline on the ground or in the air, or when play has been stopped by the referee, or when it touches a match official, remains on the field and a promising attack or a change of possession or a goal results. Crucially, the whole of the ball must cross the whole of the line. A ball overhanging the line, however far, is still in play, which is why goal-line technology exists and why an assistant referee standing level with the line is essential. At all other times the ball is in play, including when it rebounds off a goalpost, crossbar, corner flagpost or a match official and stays on the field. 

If play is stopped for a reason not covered by another Law, or the ball touches an official in the circumstances listed, the restart is a dropped ball. Since 2019 the dropped ball is no longer contested: it is given to the goalkeeper in their own penalty area if the stoppage occurred there, and otherwise to the one player of the team that last touched the ball, at the point of the last touch, with all other players of both teams at least four metres away until it is in play. That change removed the manufactured scramble and the awkward etiquette of deliberately returning the ball after a stoppage.

sections.heading: Scoring, Results and Ways of Deciding a Tie
sections.body:
A goal is scored when the whole of the ball passes over the whole of the goal line between the goalposts and beneath the crossbar, provided that no offence has been committed by the scoring team beforehand. The team scoring the greater number of goals wins; if both score the same number, or neither scores, the match is drawn. Nothing else counts. Football has no partial scores, no points for near misses and no reward for territorial dominance, which is the structural reason it produces more upsets than higher-scoring sports: a typical professional match yields fewer than three goals in total, so a single deflection carries an enormous share of the outcome. 

There is one important prohibition. A goal cannot be scored directly from a throw-in; if the ball goes into the opponents' goal a goal kick is awarded, and if into the thrower's own goal a corner kick is awarded to the opponents. A goal may be scored directly from a kick-off, a goal kick, a corner kick, a free kick or a drop kick, but never from a dropped ball, which if it enters a goal untouched by a second player is restarted with a goal kick or a corner kick as appropriate. 

When a competition needs a winner from a drawn match, the Laws recognise three permitted procedures, chosen by competition rules. Away goals, under which the team scoring more goals away from home over a two-legged tie advances, was used for decades and has been progressively abandoned since the early 2020s on the grounds that travel and pitch conditions no longer justify it. Extra time consists of two further equal periods of not more than 15 minutes each, with a short drinks interval but no proper break between them, and an additional substitution is normally permitted. The golden goal and silver goal experiments of the late 1990s, in which the first goal in extra time ended the match, were tried at major tournaments and then discarded because they encouraged extreme caution. 

The final resort is kicks from the penalty mark, commonly called a penalty shoot-out, which is formally not part of the match and whose goals are not added to the score. Both teams take five kicks alternately unless one establishes a lead the other cannot reach. If still level, the same procedure continues one pair of kicks at a time until one team scores and the other does not. Only players on the field at the end of play may take part, and before a player takes a second kick every eligible player on that team must have taken one. If one team ends the match with more players than the other, the larger team must reduce to equate, a rule that prevents a dismissal from becoming an advantage. The referee tosses a coin for the goal to be used, and a second toss decides which team kicks first; since 2017 the team winning that toss may choose to go first or second.

sections.heading: The Offside Law
sections.body:
Offside, Law 11, is the single rule that gives football its shape, and it is the one most often misunderstood, because it is really two separate tests applied at two separate moments. The first test asks about position. A player is in an offside position if any part of the head, body or feet is in the opponents' half, not counting the halfway line itself, and is nearer to the opponents' goal line than both the ball and the second-last opponent. Hands and arms are excluded from the measurement up to the bottom of the armpit, because those parts cannot legally score. The second-last opponent is usually the last outfield defender with the goalkeeper behind, but not always: if the goalkeeper has advanced, the second-last opponent may be an outfield player. Being level with the second-last opponent, or level with the last two opponents, is not an offside position. 

The second test asks about involvement, and it is judged at the exact moment a teammate plays or touches the ball, not at the moment the offside player receives it. Being in an offside position is not in itself an offence. It becomes an offence only if, at that moment, the player becomes involved in active play in one of three ways: by interfering with play, meaning playing or touching the ball passed or touched by a teammate; by interfering with an opponent, which covers preventing an opponent playing the ball by clearly obstructing their line of vision, challenging for the ball, making an obvious action that clearly impacts an opponent, or making an obvious attempt to play a ball close by that impacts an opponent; or by gaining an advantage from a ball that has rebounded or been deflected off a goalpost, crossbar, match official or opponent, or from a deliberate save. 

Two categories of contact by a defender reset the situation. If a defender deliberately plays the ball, other than a deliberate save, a player in an offside position is no longer penalised for receiving it. If a defender merely deflects the ball, or makes a deliberate save, the offside offence stands. The distinction between a deliberate play and a deflection turns on whether the defender had control of the option and time to make a considered action, and it is genuinely one of the hardest judgements in the game. 

There is no offside offence if a player receives the ball directly from a goal kick, a corner kick or a throw-in, and no offside in a player's own half. The free kick for an offside offence is indirect and is taken from the place where the offence occurred, including inside the offending player's own half. The Law's history is instructive: until 1925 three opponents had to be nearer the goal line, and reducing that number to two produced an immediate scoring explosion, from about 4,700 goals in the English First Division in 1924 to 25 to more than 6,300 the following season, and it forced the tactical invention of the centre-back.

sections.heading: Fouls: Direct and Indirect Free Kicks
sections.body:
Law 12 divides offences into those punished by a direct free kick, from which a goal may be scored immediately, and those punished by an indirect free kick, from which the ball must touch another player before a goal counts. The distinction matters enormously in and around the penalty area, because a direct free kick offence committed by a defender inside their own penalty area is punished by a penalty kick, while an indirect free kick offence there is not. 

A direct free kick is awarded when a player commits any of seven physical offences against an opponent in a manner the referee considers careless, reckless or using excessive force: charging, jumping at, kicking or attempting to kick, pushing, striking or attempting to strike including head-butting, tackling or challenging, and tripping or attempting to trip. Careless means showing a lack of attention or consideration, and carries no disciplinary sanction. Reckless means acting with disregard to the danger to, or consequences for, an opponent, and must be cautioned with a yellow card. Using excessive force means exceeding the necessary use of force and endangering the safety of an opponent, and must be punished by dismissal. These three gradations are the spine of football's disciplinary system and are worth memorising, because almost every argument about a challenge is really an argument about which of the three applies. 

A direct free kick is also awarded for holding, impeding an opponent with contact, biting or spitting at anyone, throwing an object at the ball, an opponent or an official, and for handling the ball. The handball Law was substantially rewritten between 2019 and 2021 and now turns on three ideas: a deliberate act of moving the hand or arm towards the ball; making the body unnaturally bigger by having the arm above shoulder height or extended beyond a position justified by the body's movement; and scoring directly from the hand or arm, or immediately after the ball has touched the scorer's own hand or arm, which is an offence even when entirely accidental. Accidental contact by a teammate in the build-up is no longer an offence, a correction made in 2021 after the earlier text produced widely disliked disallowed goals. 

Indirect free kicks cover playing in a dangerous manner without contact, such as a high boot near a lowered head; impeding the progress of an opponent without contact; dissent, offensive language and other verbal offences; preventing the goalkeeper releasing the ball from the hands; and a set of goalkeeper-specific offences. All free kicks are taken from where the offence occurred, with opponents at least 9.15 metres away until the ball is in play, and since 2019 attacking players must stay at least one metre from a defensive wall of three or more players. A free kick to the defending team inside its own penalty area is in play as soon as it is kicked and clearly moves, and opponents must be outside the area until then.

sections.heading: Cautions, Dismissals and Disciplinary Sanctions
sections.body:
Football's disciplinary vocabulary is two coloured cards, introduced by the English referee Ken Aston, who reportedly conceived them while stopped at traffic lights after a 1966 World Cup quarter-final in which two Argentine players had not understood they were being sent off. They were used at the 1970 World Cup and have been universal since. A yellow card is a caution; a red card is a dismissal, and a dismissed player must leave the field and its surroundings and cannot be replaced, so the team plays short for the remainder of the match. Two cautions in the same match produce a second yellow and an automatic red. 

The cautionable offences are a closed list worth knowing precisely: delaying the restart of play; dissent by word or action; entering, re-entering or deliberately leaving the field without the referee's permission; failing to respect the required distance at a corner kick, free kick or throw-in; persistent offences, with no fixed number specified; and unsporting behaviour, which is the broad category covering shirt-pulling to stop an attack, simulation, handling to stop a promising attack, and excessive celebration such as removing the shirt or climbing a perimeter fence. A player who is cautioned or sent off before entering the field, or after leaving it, is still liable, and offences committed off the field against anyone including officials and spectators are punishable. 

The sending-off offences are likewise a closed list: denying the opposing team a goal or an obvious goal-scoring opportunity by a deliberate handball, other than by a goalkeeper in their own penalty area; denying an obvious goal-scoring opportunity to an opponent moving towards the goal by an offence punishable by a free kick; serious foul play; biting or spitting at someone; violent conduct; using offensive, insulting or abusive language or gestures; and receiving a second caution. Serious foul play means a challenge that endangers an opponent's safety or uses excessive force while contesting the ball; violent conduct is force or brutality used when not contesting the ball, and can be committed against a teammate, an official or a spectator. 

Assessing an obvious goal-scoring opportunity, universally abbreviated to DOGSO, follows four published considerations: the distance between the offence and the goal, the general direction of play, the likelihood of keeping or gaining control of the ball, and the location and number of defenders. Since 2016 the so-called triple punishment has been mitigated: if the offence is an attempt to play the ball and occurs inside the offender's penalty area, the penalty kick already restores the goal-scoring chance, so the player is cautioned rather than sent off. Holding, pulling, pushing, no attempt to play the ball, or an offence punishable by a red card regardless of position still means dismissal. Suspensions following a red card are set by competition rules, not by the Laws, and commonly run from one match for a second caution to three or more for violent conduct.

sections.heading: Restarts: Throw-Ins, Goal Kicks, Corner Kicks and Advantage
sections.body:
When the ball wholly crosses a touchline the restart is a throw-in, awarded to the opponents of the player who last touched it. The technique is prescribed with unusual specificity because it would otherwise become a throwing contest: the thrower must face the field, have part of each foot on the touchline or on the ground outside it, hold the ball with both hands, and deliver it from behind and over the head from the point where it left the field. All opponents must stand at least two metres from the point of the throw. The thrower may not touch the ball again until it has touched another player, and a goal cannot be scored directly. There is no offside from a throw-in, which is why long throws into the penalty area became a specialist weapon. 

When the ball wholly crosses the goal line having last touched a player of the attacking team, and a goal is not scored, the restart is a goal kick, taken from anywhere within the goal area by any player of the defending team. The 2019 revision was significant: the ball is now in play as soon as it is kicked and clearly moves, and it no longer has to leave the penalty area. Opponents must remain outside the penalty area until then, but a team may legally pass the ball to a defender standing inside its own six-yard box. That single change did more to reshape modern build-up play than any other recent amendment, because it let goalkeepers begin attacks from the edge of the goal area against a high press. 

When the ball wholly crosses the goal line having last touched a player of the defending team, the restart is a corner kick from within the corner arc nearest where it crossed. The flagpost must not be moved, opponents must be at least 9.15 metres from the arc until the ball is in play, and a goal may be scored directly, including against the kicker's own team, in which case a corner is awarded to the opponents. As with all restarts the kicker may not play the ball a second time until someone else has touched it. 

The most consequential piece of refereeing discretion is not a restart at all but the advantage clause. The referee may allow play to continue when an offence has occurred if the offended team would benefit more from the continuation, and may return to and penalise the original offence if the anticipated advantage does not materialise within a few seconds. Signalling advantage does not cancel any disciplinary sanction: a reckless challenge still earns its yellow card at the next stoppage, and an offence that denies an obvious goal-scoring opportunity but from which a goal is nevertheless scored is reduced to a caution. Judging advantage well is what separates competent from good referees, because stopping a flowing attack to award a free kick thirty metres further back punishes the wronged team twice.

sections.heading: The Penalty Kick and the Goalkeeper's Duel
sections.body:
A penalty kick is awarded when a player commits a direct free kick offence inside their own penalty area, or off the field as part of play, while the ball is in play. It is the single most valuable set piece in the sport: conversion rates in senior professional football sit at roughly three in four, and have been remarkably stable at that level for decades, which means a penalty is worth about 0.75 of a goal against an open-play shot worth perhaps a tenth of that. 

The ball is placed on the penalty mark, 11 metres from the goal line. The kicker must be clearly identified. The defending goalkeeper must remain on the goal line facing the kicker, between the posts, without touching the goalposts, crossbar or net, and at the moment the kick is taken must have at least part of one foot touching, in line with, or behind the goal line. That wording, adopted in 2019, deliberately relaxed the old requirement that both feet stay on the line, acknowledging that goalkeepers naturally move as they dive. Every other player must be on the field, outside the penalty area, behind the penalty mark, and at least 9.15 metres from it, which is the purpose of the arc drawn outside the area. 

The kicker must kick the ball forward, may use a backheel provided the ball travels forward, and may not touch it again until another player has. Feinting in the run-up is permitted; feinting after completing the run-up is an offence, punished by a caution and an indirect free kick to the defending team even if a goal results. If the goalkeeper offends and the kick is missed or saved, the kick is retaken and the goalkeeper is warned for a first offence and cautioned for repeats; if the goalkeeper offends and a goal is scored, the goal stands. If an attacking teammate encroaches and a goal is scored, the kick is retaken; if a defending teammate encroaches and the kick is missed, it is retaken. If both teams encroach, the kick is retaken regardless of outcome. 

Tactically the penalty is a game of commitment under time pressure. A well-struck ball travels the 11 metres in roughly 0.4 to 0.5 seconds, and a goalkeeper needs about 0.6 seconds to move from a standing start to a post, so a keeper who waits until the ball is struck cannot reach the corners. The consequence is that keepers must anticipate, and kickers face a choice between a placed shot into a corner, which a guessing keeper may reach, and a hard shot down the middle, which succeeds only if the keeper has already committed. Goalkeepers who delay their dive, sometimes called staying big, force the kicker to aim precisely and are the reason the modern technique of waiting for the keeper to move, the so-called paradinha or stutter, is so tightly regulated.

sections.heading: The Goalkeeper: Special Rights and Restrictions
sections.body:
The goalkeeper is the only player permitted to handle the ball, and that permission is bounded in space and time. Handling is allowed only inside the goalkeeper's own penalty area and only while the ball is in play. Outside the area the goalkeeper is an ordinary outfield player, and handling there is a direct free kick offence, punished by dismissal if it denies an obvious goal-scoring opportunity. The goalkeeper must wear colours distinguishable from both teams' outfield players and from the match officials, and may change places with any outfield player during a stoppage provided the referee is informed.
