It declines faster with age than strength does and is trained by moving moderate loads fast, not by slow grinding. **Flexibility and mobility** are range of motion, passive and active. **Body composition** is the proportion of fat to lean tissue. ⚠️ It is worth stating plainly that exercise is a comparatively weak tool for weight loss on its own — appetite compensates for much of what is burned — while it is an excellent tool for **maintaining** weight, preserving muscle during weight loss, and improving health markers substantially **even when weight does not change**. Fitness and fatness are partly independent, and improving fitness carries benefits regardless. **Balance and coordination** are trainable and matter enormously with age, since falls are a leading cause of serious injury in older adults. Standing on one leg, heel-to-toe walking, and activities like dancing, tai chi and racket sports all train them. **Intensity and how to judge it without equipment.** The **talk test** is the most practical: full conversation is easy, a few words at a time is vigorous, cannot speak is maximal. **Rating of perceived exertion** on a 1–10 scale is nearly as good as a heart-rate monitor for most purposes. Heart-rate zones are useful but the familiar "220 minus age" formula for maximum heart rate is a rough population average with a wide error, so zones built on it are approximate. **Interval training** — repeated hard efforts with recovery — improves both endurance and the ability to tolerate hard work, and is time-efficient. ⚠️ It is also the highest-injury, highest- fatigue form of training, so it belongs on top of an established base rather than at the start.

sections.heading: Exercise Across a Life: Age, Pregnancy and Chronic Conditions
sections.body: The general principles hold throughout life; what changes is the emphasis and the cautions. **Children and adolescents** benefit from far more activity than adults — around an hour a day of moderate to vigorous movement is the usual recommendation — mostly through play and sport, with activities that load bone, such as running and jumping, being especially valuable while the skeleton is developing. ⚠️ Resistance training is safe and beneficial for young people with competent supervision and technique-first progression; the old belief that it stunts growth is not supported. The genuine risk is **early specialisation** in a single sport, which is associated with overuse injury and burnout. **Older adults** should do everything already described, plus **balance training**, and should weight **strength and power** more heavily rather than less. Muscle mass and, especially, power decline with age, and that decline is what removes independence — the ability to rise from a chair, climb stairs and recover from a stumble. It is trainable at every age, including into the nineties. Weight-bearing and resistance work also help maintain bone density. **Pregnancy.** Activity is generally recommended rather than merely permitted, with benefits for blood-pressure disorders, gestational diabetes and mood. The usual guidance is to continue what you were doing, adapted, and to start gently if you were not. ⚠️ Sensible cautions: avoid contact sports and activities with a fall risk, avoid scuba diving, avoid overheating, and be aware that prolonged flat-on-the-back exercise becomes uncomfortable and is generally avoided later on. Pelvic floor work matters. ⚠️ Stop and seek advice for bleeding, regular painful contractions, fluid leak, breathlessness before exertion, chest pain, headache, dizziness or calf pain and swelling. Anyone with pregnancy complications should be guided by their clinician. **Common chronic conditions.** Exercise is a first-line treatment, not a risk, for a long list of them, though the specifics belong with a clinician: - **Type 2 diabetes**: improves insulin sensitivity markedly. ⚠️ Those on insulin or sulfonylureas must plan for hypoglycaemia during and after. - **Hypertension and heart disease**: strongly beneficial; **supervised cardiac rehabilitation** is the standard route after a cardiac event. - **Osteoarthritis**: exercise reduces pain and improves function. The instinct to rest a painful joint indefinitely makes it worse. - **Back pain**: staying active and returning to normal movement beats bed rest decisively. - **Asthma**: exercise is encouraged, with a reliever available and attention to warm-up and cold air. - **Osteoporosis**: weight-bearing and resistance work help; ⚠️ heavy spinal flexion and twisting under load are usually cautioned against. - **Depression and anxiety**: exercise has consistent, meaningful effects on mood.

sections.heading: Sport: Skill, Practice and Getting Better at a Game
sections.body: Training for fitness and getting better at a sport overlap and are not the same, because a sport is a skill and skills are learned by different rules than fitness is built by. **Specificity.** Adaptation is specific to the demand. A cyclist's fitness transfers to running only partly; a strong squatter is not automatically a good jumper. Fitness work supports a sport; the sport itself is what makes you good at it. **How skills are actually learned.** Three findings from motor-learning research are consistently useful and consistently ignored: - **Blocked practice flatters, random practice teaches.** Hitting fifty identical shots feels productive and produces less retention than mixing shots unpredictably. Performance during practice and learning that survives to next week are different things, and the arrangement that looks worse in the session is often better in the long run. - **An external focus beats an internal one.** Attention on the effect — the target, the ball's flight, pushing the ground away — produces better results than attention on your own body parts. - **Feedback should be occasional, not constant.** Being told what happened after every attempt creates dependence; less frequent, summary feedback produces better retention. **Deliberate practice** is the concept behind rapid improvement: purposeful work at the edge of current ability, on a specific weakness, with feedback and correction — as distinct from simply playing, which maintains what you already do. Most people improve slowly because they play rather than practise. **Learning stages.** Early on, movement is conscious, effortful and inconsistent, and improvement is rapid. With practice it becomes smoother and less variable. Eventually it becomes automatic and attention is freed for tactics and for reading opponents — which is why experts appear to have more time. **Warm-up injury-prevention programmes.** Structured neuromuscular warm-ups — jogging, strength work, plyometrics, balance and landing technique, done regularly before training — have good evidence for reducing lower-limb injuries in team sports, particularly knee and hamstring injuries. They take about fifteen minutes and are among the best-supported interventions in sport. **Load management.** Sharp spikes in training or competition load are associated with injury; the consistent theme is that a well-built base tolerates more, and sudden increases after a break are the danger point. Returning after time out means rebuilding, not resuming where you stopped. ⚠️ **Head injury deserves a rule of its own**: any suspected concussion means removal from play that day, with no return until assessed and cleared. Continuing to play with a concussion, or returning too early, is the circumstance in which the rare catastrophic outcomes occur.

sections.heading: Building a Week That You Will Actually Do
sections.body: The gap between knowing what to do and doing it is where almost all failure happens, and it is a practical problem with practical answers. **Design around your constraints first.** Decide how many days you can genuinely commit to on a bad week, not a good one, and build for that. A three-day plan you complete beats a five-day plan you complete three days of, because the second one also teaches you that you are failing. **A workable general week** for someone with general health as the goal: two resistance sessions covering the main movement patterns, two or three easy-to-moderate cardiovascular sessions, daily walking, and some mobility work. That fits inside the standard public guidance and takes under three hours. **Order within a session.** If you are doing both in one session, do the priority first. Strength before endurance if strength is the goal; the reverse if endurance is. Skill and power work go early, when you are fresh, because they are degraded by fatigue. **Make it concrete.** "Exercise more" fails; "Monday, Wednesday and Friday at seven, gym bag by the door" works. **Implementation intentions** — deciding in advance exactly when, where and what, and what you will do if the plan breaks — are among the best-supported behaviour-change techniques there are. So is **habit stacking**: attaching the new activity to something already fixed in your day. **Reduce friction.** Prepare kit the night before. Choose the gym you pass anyway rather than the better one across town. Have an indoor fallback for bad weather. Every removed obstacle raises the odds more than motivation does, because motivation is not reliably available and systems are. **Track something, lightly.** A simple record of sessions completed is enough, and seeing an unbroken run is itself motivating. ⚠️ Do not let tracking become the point — abandoning a session because it will not be logged, or chasing a device's daily target while injured, is the tail wagging the dog. **Expect to miss sessions, and plan the response.** The people who succeed are not the ones who never miss; they are the ones who resume immediately without treating a missed week as failure. The **never-miss-twice** rule is the practical form. **Company helps.** Training with someone, joining a club, or a class at a fixed time all add accountability. Parkrun-style free community events and beginner groups exist almost everywhere and solve the two hardest problems at once — a fixed time, and other beginners. **Finally, define success as showing up.** Performance fluctuates with sleep, stress, illness and life. Attendance is the variable you control, and over a year it is the one that determines everything else.

sections.heading: Equipment, a Home Gym, and Spending Money Sensibly
sections.body: Fitness is an industry, and most of what it sells is optional. Knowing what genuinely helps saves money and, more importantly, removes excuses. **What actually matters.** Footwear that fits and is comfortable for what you do. Clothing you can move in and that suits your climate. For strength, something to progressively load with. That is close to the whole list. **Home versus gym.** A gym provides equipment range, heavier loads, staff, classes and other people; home provides zero travel time and zero self-consciousness. The travel time is not trivial — a gym twenty minutes away costs forty minutes per session, which is often the difference between going and not. ⚠️ For beginners, the deciding factor is usually not equipment but whether you will turn up. **A capable home setup, cheaply**, in order of value for money: your own body weight, which progresses a long way through leverage and repetitions; a set of **resistance bands**; a pair of **adjustable dumbbells** or kettlebells; a **pull-up bar**; a mat. Add a bench and a barbell with a rack only if you know you want heavy free-weight training. **Second-hand** is the sensible default for weights, which are essentially indestructible, and often for cardio machines, of which a great many are sold barely used. **Wearables and apps.** Step counters and heart-rate monitors are genuinely useful for making activity visible and pacing effort. ⚠️ Treat their derived numbers with scepticism: calorie estimates in particular can be substantially wrong, sleep staging is approximate, and "recovery scores" are proprietary composites, not measurements. Use trends rather than absolute values. **Coaching is the underrated purchase.** A few sessions with a competent coach at the start of strength training or swimming will improve technique and safety more than any equipment, and the cost is small compared with a year's membership. Check qualifications and insurance; the industry is unevenly regulated. **Supplements.** The overwhelming majority are unnecessary if you eat adequately. A small number have reasonable evidence for specific purposes — creatine monohydrate for strength and power, caffeine for performance, protein powder purely as a convenient food, and vitamin D where sunlight exposure is low or deficiency is documented. ⚠️ Anything promising rapid fat loss or dramatic muscle gain is either ineffective or a drug, and the supplement market is poorly regulated in most countries, with contamination a real and repeatedly documented problem for anyone subject to drug testing. **Classes and group training** buy structure, a fixed time and instruction. ⚠️ Their weakness is that a class cannot scale to individuals, so a beginner in an intense class is the classic too-much-too-soon case. Tell the instructor you are new, and take the easier option offered.

sections.heading: Common Injuries — Shin Splints, Runner's Knee, Tendinopathy — and When to Stop
sections.body: Most exercise injuries are not dramatic accidents. They are gradual overuse problems that gave warning for weeks, and knowing the warnings is what separates a fortnight's setback from a six-month one. **Acute versus overuse.** An **acute** injury has a moment — a sprain, a strain, a fall. An **overuse** injury accumulates from repeated load without adequate recovery, and it typically follows a change: more distance, new shoes, new surface, new exercise, a return after a break. ⚠️ **Whenever something hurts, ask what changed in the past two to four weeks.** The answer is usually there. **Early management of an acute soft-tissue injury.** Current guidance has moved away from the old RICE advice toward protecting the area briefly, then **loading it early and progressively** — prolonged rest delays recovery. Ice may ease pain; its effect on healing is doubtful. Elevation and compression help swelling. ⚠️ Avoid heat, alcohol and vigorous massage in the first day or two, which can increase bleeding and swelling. **Frequent problems and their usual cause:** - **Shin splints**: too much running volume too quickly, especially on hard surfaces. - **Runner's knee**: pain around the kneecap, often load-related; typically responds to reducing volume and strengthening hips and thighs. - **Achilles tendinopathy**: gradual-onset pain and stiffness at the tendon, worst in the morning. Managed with progressive loading, not rest alone. - **Plantar heel pain**: sharp under-heel pain on the first steps of the day. - **Tennis and golfer's elbow**: gripping and repetitive loading; not confined to those sports. - **Rotator cuff and shoulder impingement**: often from overhead volume with weak scapular control. - **Low back pain**: extremely common, usually not serious, and best managed by staying active. - **Stress fractures**: localised bone pain that worsens with impact and is tender to press. ⚠️ These need diagnosis and rest from impact; training through one risks a complete fracture. ⚠️ **Stop immediately and seek urgent medical help** for chest pain or pressure, especially with breathlessness, sweating or arm or jaw pain; sudden severe headache; fainting or near-fainting; sudden one-sided weakness or slurred speech; a joint that has visibly deformed; an audible pop with immediate inability to bear weight; or calf pain and swelling at rest, which can indicate a clot. **Returning after injury.** Return when the tissue tolerates load without pain increasing during or afterwards, progressing gradually and restoring range and strength before speed and impact. Resuming at your pre-injury level is the reliable route to re-injury, and reinjury is more common than the original.

sections.heading: What Exercise Actually Does to You
sections.body: The reason any of this is worth doing is that the physiological effects are large, broad and unusually well established, and they are worth knowing plainly rather than as marketing. **The heart and circulation.** Endurance training increases the heart's stroke volume, so it pumps more per beat and works at a lower rate at rest and at any given effort. Blood volume rises, capillary networks in trained muscle expand, and blood vessels become better at dilating. Blood pressure falls modestly and consistently, and lipid profiles improve. **Muscles.** Endurance training multiplies mitochondria and improves the muscle's capacity to use fat and oxygen, which is much of what raises endurance. Resistance training increases the size and force of muscle fibres and, early on, improves neural recruitment. Both improve **insulin sensitivity**: contracting muscle takes up glucose by a pathway that does not require insulin, which is why exercise works for type 2 diabetes and why the effect of a single session lasts roughly a day or two — and why regularity matters more than duration. **Bone.** Bone remodels in response to load, so impact and resistance work build and maintain density while inactivity loses it. The window of youth and early adulthood, when peak bone mass is being set, matters lifelong. **The brain.** Exercise improves mood and reduces symptoms of depression and anxiety with reasonable consistency, improves sleep quality, and is associated with better cognitive function and reduced dementia risk in later life. Mechanisms proposed include increased blood flow, neurotrophic factors, and effects on inflammation and stress hormones. **Immunity and inflammation.** Regular moderate activity is associated with fewer and shorter infections; very heavy training without recovery appears to work the other way. Chronic low-grade inflammation, implicated in many diseases of ageing, is reduced. **Metabolism and appetite.** Energy expenditure rises during and briefly after exercise, and lean mass raises resting expenditure a little. ⚠️ Appetite and unconscious movement compensate for a substantial share of what is burned, which is the honest reason exercise alone is an inefficient weight-loss tool while remaining an excellent health tool. **Ageing.** Much of what is attributed to age — lost muscle, lost power, lost balance, lost aerobic capacity, lost bone — is partly disuse, and partly reversible at any age. This is the single most encouraging finding in the field. **The size of the effect.** Physical inactivity is among the leading modifiable risk factors for death worldwide, and cardiorespiratory fitness is one of the strongest predictors of survival there is — comparable to or stronger than the conventional risk factors. Very few interventions available to an ordinary person do as much, and the largest gains come from the first steps away from doing nothing.
